At a meeting in Hardin on November 20, 1975, the Admiristrative Officer of the Coal Board stated that a 10 percent population growth in three years would qualify as an indication of the necessary severity of impact. A recent estimate by the Department of Community Affairs indicates a 21.5 percent population increase in Hardin since 1970 (Hardin Herald, November 27, 1975, p. 1). Rusty Rokita (personal communication, January 8, 1976) stated that it is widely recognized that Hardin, Forsyth, and Colstrip have received the largest impacts from coal, and that some funding is likely. However, the actions of the Coal Board cannot be anticipated; it is their option to award from 0 to 17.5 percent of tax receipts. The amount of aid which Hardin and the school districts receive will depend on how the Coal Board chooses to define the legislative intent of the bill.
Private Services Impacts
As population increases in the Impact Area, additional private services will be needed. There will be some increased demand for dentists, optometrists, medical doctors, and nursing homes, as well as some expansion of natural gas and electricity services. The demand for these services will be made only slightly larger by the presence of mining on the Westmoreland Resources lease tracts. Retail services are also expected to increase to meet the demands of a larger market, bringing added vitality to present business centers.
